chapters: The woman whom You gave me
The way to the tree of life

events.text: The garden as The Garden left it: Eden in full morning light, the two far off among the trees, at peace. Then, low in the grass at the edge of the frame, something moves.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The last chapter ended with a man and a woman naked and unashamed in a good garden. This chapter answers the question every reader eventually asks: if the world began like that, why is it like this?
THE FALL / Genesis 3:1 to 24
The grass is still again. Music opens, darker than before.
Long grass at the foot of the trees; a small snake, far off and half hidden, moving through the grass toward the centre of the garden.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The chapter opens with a pun English cannot keep. The pair were naked, arummim. The serpent is crafty, arum. The two words sound almost the same.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The ancient world wove the snake into its royal and sacred imagery. Genesis calls it simply a creature the LORD God had made. But later Scripture names the enemy behind the voice:

events.speaker: READER
events.text: that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: He never commands. He only asks, and his first move is a question about what God said.

The tree in the middle of the garden, seen from far off between the trunks of other trees; beneath it, very small, the woman in profile; the snake low in the grass near her, a thin dark line, far off.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.’”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: God gave every tree freely and set one limit. She drops the freely, adds touching, and softens the warning. She shrinks the gift and enlarges the limit.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: “You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: “For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The serpent takes God's own warning and puts a not in front of it. He contradicts God word for word, and paints the Giver of every tree as jealous. The root of sin, as Genesis tells it, is not ignorance but distrust.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Notice too that the narrator says the LORD God, His covenant name, but in this conversation they say only God. The personal name drops out just as trust in Him is dissolving.
The tree in the middle of the garden in warm light, heavy with fruit of no particular kind; two very small figures beneath it, far off, framed by branches. Nothing close.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: This is the only window the narrator gives into her mind, and it climbs. Good for food: the appetite. Pleasing to the eyes: the eye. Desirable for wisdom: ambition.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Desirable is the verb of the tenth commandment, you shall not covet. What God made to be enjoyed becomes something to be seized. And the man was with her, saying nothing at all.
Broad fig leaves in the foreground, dark against the evening light; far beyond them, two tiny figures withdrawn into the shade of the trees.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Their eyes are opened, but what they see is their own exposure. One act fractures every relationship at once, and shame arrives before any sentence is spoken. The fig leaves are their own attempt to cover it.
Evening in the garden. Wind moves through the treetops in a long wave, and light shifts across the ground between the trunks, as though something passes through. No figure anywhere.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Walking is the verb later used for God's presence moving through Israel's camp. And they hide from Him among the very trees He planted.
Deep among dark trunks, the evening light moving through the leaves toward the place where the two are hidden, far off and unseen.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: But the LORD God called out to the man,

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Where are you?”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Many readers see this question at the centre of the chapter. The turning point is not the eating but the God who comes looking. He knows where they are. He asks so that the guilty will speak the truth.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: “I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.text: The garden in failing light; two far off figures half hidden among dark trunks; in the low grass between the trees, the snake lies still.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Who told you that you were naked?”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: asked the LORD God.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: And the man answered, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The man said nothing until he was questioned, and now he speaks to excuse himself.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: Then the LORD God said to the woman,

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “What is this you have done?”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: “The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The sin travelled from serpent to woman to man. The blame is passed back down the line. What she says is true, but it is not a defence.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And God questions the man and the woman, but puts no question to the serpent. He does not negotiate with evil. He sentences it.
Bare dust at the edge of the garden in low light; the snake, small and far off, going on its belly through the dust. Wind over the ground.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: So the LORD God said to the serpent:

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field! On your belly will you go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Cursed falls on the serpent, and on the ground, never on the man or the woman themselves. Even in Isaiah's renewed world, this one sentence stands:

events.speaker: READER
events.text: the food of the serpent will be dust
Dawn breaking low over the dust at the garden's edge; a single line of gold light falling across the ground; the snake gone into shadow.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Enmity means open war. The rescue of the world begins as God's declaration of war on evil.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: One verb stands behind both blows: the head against the heel, a fatal blow against a wounding one. And the seed is he. A long war between two lines, but the decisive blow is struck by one.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: This is the first announcement of the gospel, spoken before a single sentence falls on the man and the woman.
The garden under a heavy sky at dusk, wind bending the long grass; no figures.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: To the woman He said:

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Her pain is the same word as the man's toil. And the desire and the rule describe a marriage bent by sin, not God's design: a sorrowful description of the world under judgment, never a charter for it.
Beyond the trees, a hard field under a hot sky; thorns and thistles rising from cracked ground; dry wind lifting the dust.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And to Adam He said:

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground, because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Chapter two ran from dust to a living man. Chapter three runs that film backward: the man taken from the ground will return to it.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Yet mercy is laced through the judgment. Childbearing continues, so the promised seed can still come. Work continues, so life goes on.
First light over the garden after the night; far off among the trees, two small figures standing together; nothing close.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Eve sounds like the Hebrew for living. In the very hour death enters, a small act of hope in God's promise.
Simple garments of skin resting in warm light at the foot of a tree; far beyond, the two small figures among the trunks.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The fig leaves were their own covering. These garments are God's, and the words are the ones used when Moses clothed Israel's priests.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The text does not describe a sacrifice, so the link is an inference, but a fair one: the covering came from a life taken.
The tree of life at the far centre of the garden in soft light, seen from a great distance through the trees; wind in the leaves; no figure.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Then the LORD God said,

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Even the exile is a mercy. It guards them from living forever in a fallen state.

The eastern edge of the garden at dusk: two very small figures walking away east into a wide dry land, seen from behind, far off; behind them, in the opening between the trees, a slow turning flame of light.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: To Israel this sounded like being barred from the sanctuary: its door faced east, and cherubim were worked into the veil before the Most Holy Place.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And east becomes a direction in Genesis. Cain settles east of Eden. Babel's builders journey east. Humanity keeps moving away from the presence it lost.
A wilderness of stone and dry hills at first light, empty, no figures.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Verse fifteen does not name the victor. The promise narrows to Abraham, then to David, and comes to rest on one person. God sent His Son, Paul says,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: born of a woman

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Luke traces Jesus back to Adam, and the next scene is the temptation. The last Adam meets the same enemy in a wilderness, hungry, and answers with what God said. He wins where the first man lost.
An olive grove at night across a dry stream bed; then a rock cut tomb in a garden at first light, the stone rolled back; no figures.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Adam hid among the trees. Christ was hung on a tree. Adam reached for what was forbidden. Christ, in a garden, prayed:

events.speaker: READER
events.text: not as I will, but as You will

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Adam wore thorns as the fruit of his sin; Christ wore them as a crown. Adam left the garden to die; Christ was laid in a garden tomb, and rose. And the promise never pictured a victory without cost. He shared our flesh and blood,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The strike to the heel and the crushing of the head happen in the same act.

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.text: A great woven curtain torn from top to bottom, warm light pouring through the tear; then a radiant city with a river, and the tree of life on both banks.

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: When Jesus died, the veil with its cherubim was torn from top to bottom. Believers now come in

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.speaker: READER
events.text: by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The Bible closes by undoing this chapter. No longer any curse. The tree of life open beside the river. And the pair who hid from God are answered by a people who

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.speaker: READER
events.text: will see His face

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.text: Back in the garden at evening: wind in the trees, light moving gently between the trunks.

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: So hear God's questions as grace. Do not hide or blame. Come out and confess, and trust the God who promised a Rescuer and clothed the naked.

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: God covered their shame with garments He provided. What are you using to cover your own shame, and what would it mean to receive God's covering in Christ instead?

events.chapter: The way to the tree of life
events.text: Hold on the light. Music resolves.
